To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

depth-dependent extension results either in two-stage breakup with necking of the crust followed by necking of the mantle lithosphere or vice versa, with the style of the associated sediment basin being a consequence of the order of breakup.
the observed properties of non-volatile rifted margins can be explained by two-stage breakup, with crustal necking or mantle-lithosphere stretching occurring first.

the two end-member styles of rifted margin, type I (e.g., Iberia–UK margin) and type II (e.g., some central South Atlantic margins) are opposite end members, resulting from two-stage breakup in which the crust or mantle lithospheric necks before the other, and the two-stage nature is a consequence of depth-dependent lithospheric extension.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the processes of lithospheric thinning and breakup of the continents and the implications of these processes for the evolution of the continental crust and the sedimentary basins that form on them.
the evolution of rifted margins, which are the sites where continental crust and mantle lithospheric are separated and where the oceanic crust is formed.
the fundamental problem of how continental margins evolve and the processes that control their structure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lithosphere behaves in a depth-dependent manner, and that two-stage breakup is the rule, not the exception.
the continental lithosphere is not uniform, and that it has different properties in the crust and in the mantle lithosphere.
the lithosphere of rifted margins is heterogeneous and has been broken up in two stages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
depth-dependent extension is a fundamental property of continental lithosphere and that the resulting two-stage breakup explains many of the characteristics of rifted margins.
the continental crust is a strong layer and the mantle lithosphere is a weak layer.
rifted margins are not all the same, and the two-stage breakup behaviour of some margins may be a result of depth-dependent extension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the crust and mantle lithospheres behave differently during continental breakup and that this difference has a significant effect on the style of breakup and its consequences for margin development.
the lithospheric architecture of rifted margins is not uniform but depends on the relative extension of the crust and mantle lithospheric components.
the crust and lithospheric mantle are coupled in extensional deformation, and their relative extensional behaviour is a key control on rift margin architecture.
